questions.passage:
Students investigated how exposed surface area affects the evaporation of water. They placed 50.0 mL of water in each of four shallow plastic trays of similar material but with different exposed surface areas. The exposed water surface areas were 25, 50, 75, and 100 cm². All trays were placed on the same table in a room kept at 24.0°C with 45% relative humidity. No fan was used. After 3.0 h, the students measured the mass lost from each tray with a balance accurate to 0.1 g. They repeated the experiment three times and calculated the mean mass lost and mean evaporation rate. The results are shown in Table 1.

Table 1
Exposed area (cm²) | Mean mass lost in 3.0 h (g) | Mean evaporation rate (g/h)
25 | 3.0 | 1.0
50 | 5.9 | 2.0
75 | 8.7 | 2.9
100 | 11.4 | 3.8

The students also noted that the trays with larger surface areas had shallower water at the start because the same volume was added to each tray. They wondered whether water depth affected the results in addition to surface area.
questions.q: According to Table 1, which exposed area had a mean evaporation rate closest to 3.0 g/h?
options: 25 cm²
75 cm²
50 cm²
100 cm²
questions.explanation: The mean evaporation rate for 75 cm² is 2.9 g/h, which is only 0.1 g/h from 3.0 g/h. The other rates are 1.0, 2.0, and 3.8 g/h, so they are farther from 3.0 g/h.

questions.q: A student claims that, over the range tested, the mean mass lost in 3.0 h is directly proportional to exposed area. Using the 25 cm² result to set the proportional model, what mass lost is predicted for an exposed area of 125 cm²?
questions.explanation: The proportional model uses 3.0 g ÷ 25 cm² = 0.12 g/cm², so 125 cm² predicts 0.12 × 125 = 15.0 g. A value such as 12.0 g would be predicted for only 100 cm² under the same model.

questions.q: Which change to the students’ setup would best control for the possible effect of water depth while still comparing different exposed surface areas?
options: Use the same 50.0 mL volume in every tray, as in the original setup.

Add different volumes of water so that all trays begin with the same water depth.
Place a lid over each tray during the 3.0 h period.

questions.q: The results in Table 1 best support which statement?
options: The mean evaporation rate decreased as exposed area increased.
The mean evaporation rate was exactly proportional to exposed area at all four areas tested.
Changing exposed area from 25 to 100 cm² had no consistent effect on mean evaporation rate.
Increasing the exposed area from 25 to 50 cm² increased the mean evaporation rate by a larger amount than increasing it from 75 to 100 cm².

questions.topic: Data representation: reading tables and graphs
questions.q:
The table shows the density of four liquids at 20°C.

Liquid | Density (g/mL)
W | 0.79
X | 0.92
Y | 1.00
Z | 1.26

A 10.0 mL sample of which liquid has a mass closest to 9.2 g?
options: Liquid X
Liquid W
Liquid Z
Liquid Y
questions.explanation: Mass equals density × volume. For liquid X, 0.92 g/mL × 10.0 mL = 9.2 g, so liquid X is closest. The other samples would have masses of 7.9 g, 10.0 g, and 12.6 g.

questions.q: A model predicts the volume V, in liters, of water in a tank after t minutes as V = 40 − 3t, for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12. According to the model, after how many minutes is the volume 19 L?
options: 5 min
8 min
6 min
7 min
questions.explanation: Set 40 − 3t = 19, so 3t = 21 and t = 7 min. At 6 min the model gives 22 L, and at 8 min it gives 16 L.

questions.q: A student wants to test whether a new paper towel brand absorbs more water than an older brand. The student soaks one sheet of each brand in 200 mL of water for 10 s, hangs the sheets to drip for 1 min, and measures the water retained. Which change would best reduce the effect of variation among individual paper towels?
options: Use only the thickest sheet from each brand.
Let one brand drip for 1 min and the other brand drip for 2 min.
Use a larger volume of water for each sheet.
Test several sheets of each brand and compare the mean water retained.
questions.explanation: Variation among individual sheets is best handled by averaging multiple sheets from each brand. Using only one selected sheet, changing water volume, or giving brands different drip times would introduce new differences rather than control variation.

questions.q:
The table shows results from an experiment measuring carbon dioxide produced by yeast in three sugar solutions.

Solution | Mean CO₂ produced (mL) | Range (mL)
Glucose | 34 | 33–35
Fructose | 31 | 25–37
Sucrose | 28 | 26–30

Which statement is best supported by the table?
options: All three sugar solutions produced equally variable results.
Sucrose produced more carbon dioxide on average than glucose.
Glucose produced a higher mean volume than sucrose, and its range was narrower than fructose's range.
Fructose produced the highest mean volume of carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: The mean for glucose is 34 mL, greater than the 28 mL mean for sucrose, and glucose's range is 2 mL while fructose's range is 12 mL. Fructose did not have the highest mean, and sucrose did not exceed glucose.

questions.q: A student recorded the mass of a crystal every 2 minutes: 10.0 g at 0 min, 12.5 g at 2 min, 15.0 g at 4 min, 16.8 g at 6 min, and 18.0 g at 8 min. Between which two consecutive times did the mass increase by the smallest amount?
options: Between 0 min and 2 min
Between 2 min and 4 min
Between 4 min and 6 min
Between 6 min and 8 min
questions.explanation: The increases are 2.5 g from 0 to 2 min, 2.5 g from 2 to 4 min, 1.8 g from 4 to 6 min, and 1.2 g from 6 to 8 min. The smallest increase is 1.2 g, between 6 and 8 min.

questions.passage:
Two researchers studied four ponds near a small farm. Dr. Rivera proposed that dissolved oxygen (DO) is mainly controlled by water temperature: warmer water holds less oxygen. Dr. Patel proposed that algae abundance is more important: algae produce oxygen during daylight but use oxygen at night, and dense algal growth can cause large daily changes in DO. On the same morning, the researchers measured DO at 6 a.m. (before sunrise) and at 2 p.m., along with mean water temperature and algae cover. Table 1 summarizes the results.

Pond | Mean water temperature (°C) | Algae cover (%) | DO at 6 a.m. (mg/L) | DO at 2 p.m. (mg/L)
1 | 18 | 10 | 7.8 | 8.1
2 | 22 | 70 | 4.9 | 9.8
3 | 22 | 5 | 7.0 | 7.3
4 | 26 | 30 | 4.6 | 5.7

Dr. Rivera notes that Pond 4 has both the warmest water and the lowest 6 a.m. DO. Dr. Patel notes that Ponds 2 and 3 have the same temperature but very different algae cover and DO changes. Neither researcher claims that only one factor is involved.
questions.q: The disagreement between Dr. Rivera and Dr. Patel centers most directly on whether:
options: Pond 4 is warmer than Ponds 2 and 3.
water temperature or algae cover has the greater influence on dissolved oxygen in the ponds.
dissolved oxygen concentrations can differ between morning and afternoon.
algae in ponds can affect dissolved oxygen during daylight.
questions.explanation: Dr. Rivera emphasizes temperature as the main control on dissolved oxygen, while Dr. Patel emphasizes algae cover as more important. The other statements are observations or common ground, not the main conflict.

questions.topic: Data representation: trends, interpolation and extrapolation
questions.q:
A student measured the volume of a gas as its temperature changed at constant pressure. The data are shown in the table.

Temperature (°C) | Volume (mL)
0 | 100
20 | 107
40 | 115
60 | 122

Using linear interpolation between 20°C and 40°C, what volume would be predicted at 30°C?
options: 108 mL
114 mL
111 mL
122 mL
questions.explanation: The 30°C point is halfway between 20°C and 40°C, so the predicted volume is halfway between 107 mL and 115 mL: (107 + 115) ÷ 2 = 111 mL.

questions.q: Two students discuss why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden spoon at room temperature. Maya says the metal must be at a lower temperature. Devin says both are at room temperature, but metal transfers heat away from the hand faster. Which observation would best support Devin's explanation?
options: The metal spoon is shinier than the wooden spoon.
Both spoons have the same mass and volume.
A thermometer reads the same temperature for both spoons, and the metal spoon warms a cold block faster.
The metal spoon has a lower reading on a thermometer than the wooden spoon.
questions.explanation: Devin claims the spoons are at the same temperature but differ in heat transfer. Equal thermometer readings support equal temperature, and the metal spoon warming a cold block faster supports faster heat transfer. A lower thermometer reading for metal would instead support Maya's claim.

questions.topic: Data representation: reading tables and graphs
questions.q:
Students recorded the number of gas bubbles produced per minute by yeast at several sugar concentrations. The data are shown in the table.

Sugar concentration (%) | Bubbles per minute
0 | 2
2 | 8
4 | 17
6 | 23
8 | 22
10 | 14

Between which two sugar concentrations is the average increase in bubbles per minute greatest per 1% increase in sugar concentration?
questions.explanation: The average increase per 1% is (17 − 8) ÷ 2 = 4.5 bubbles per minute from 2% to 4%. The values for 0% to 2% and 4% to 6% are both 3, and from 6% to 8% the number decreases, so 2% to 4% is the greatest increase.

questions.q: A model predicts the temperature of a cup of water after it is placed in a 20°C room: T = 20 + 60(0.85)^m, where T is temperature in °C and m is time in minutes. According to the model, what is the predicted decrease in temperature from minute 1 to minute 2?

questions.topic: Data representation: trends, interpolation and extrapolation
questions.q:
A diver recorded the total pressure at several depths in a lake, as shown in the table.

Depth (m) | Total pressure (kPa)
0 | 101
5 | 151
10 | 201
15 | 251

If the linear trend continues, what total pressure would be predicted at 22 m?
options: 341 kPa
321 kPa
311 kPa
301 kPa
questions.explanation: The pressure increases by 50 kPa every 5 m, which is 10 kPa per meter. At 22 m, the predicted pressure is 101 + 22 × 10 = 321 kPa.

questions.passage:
Maya, Jordan, and Priya investigated how dissolved table salt affects the time needed for an ice cube to melt in water. They prepared 200 mL of distilled water at 22°C in a 400 mL beaker. To each beaker they added sodium chloride to make solutions of 0, 10, 20, 30, or 40 g/L and stirred until no crystals remained. For each concentration, they placed one 25.0 g ice cube made in the same mold into the beaker and recorded the time until no solid ice remained. The water was not stirred during melting. Each concentration was run in three trials, and a new ice cube and fresh solution were used each time. They recorded the solution temperature at the start and end of each trial; it remained between 21°C and 23°C. The table shows the mean time and range for each concentration.
Concentration (g/L) | Mean melting time (s) | Range (s)
0 | 210 | 204–216
10 | 186 | 181–191
20 | 158 | 152–164
30 | 137 | 132–142
40 | 119 | 114–124
questions.q: Which variable was the independent variable in the students' experiment?
options: The mass of the ice cube
The concentration of sodium chloride in the water
The starting temperature of the water
The time required for the ice cube to melt completely
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the students deliberately changed, which was the sodium chloride concentration. Melting time was the measured dependent variable, while starting water temperature and ice-cube mass were held constant.

questions.q: The students used a new ice cube and fresh solution for each trial. Which change would best improve the reliability of the mean melting times?
options: Use a larger ice cube at higher concentrations.
Run five additional trials at each concentration and recalculate the mean.
Keep only the fastest trial at each concentration.
Use a different beaker size for each concentration.
questions.explanation: Running more trials improves reliability by reducing the effect of random variation in each measurement. Changing ice mass or beaker size would introduce new variables, and keeping only the fastest trial would bias the results rather than improve reliability.

questions.passage:
Two ecologists studied bee visits along a 60 m wildflower strip beside a paved road. At distances of 5, 15, 25, 35, and 45 m from the road, they counted bees visiting flowers for 1 hour on each of six warm afternoons. They also measured flower density at each distance. Dr. Nguyen claims that vehicle exhaust near the road reduces bee activity, so bee visits should increase steadily with distance from the road. Dr. Alvarez claims that bee visits are driven mainly by flower density rather than by vehicle exhaust. All counts were made between 10:00 a.m. and 2:00 p.m., when air temperature was 23°C–27°C and wind speed was below 3 m/s. No pesticides were applied to the strip during the study. The table shows the mean values.
Distance from road (m) | Mean bee visits per hour | Flower density (flowers/m²)
5 | 12 | 18
15 | 17 | 26
25 | 22 | 34
35 | 20 | 30
45 | 15 | 22
questions.q: Which statement best supports Dr. Alvarez's claim that flower density mainly determines bee visits?
options: Mean bee visits were lowest at 5 m, the distance closest to the road.
Mean bee visits increased consistently as flower density increased across the five distances.
Mean bee visits increased steadily with distance from the road.

questions.passage:
Students investigated how salt concentration in water affects radish seed germination. They placed 50 radish seeds on filter paper in separate beakers and added 20 mL of a NaCl solution at 0, 2, 4, or 8 g/L. Half of the beakers were kept in a growth chamber at 15°C and half at 25°C. Each treatment was repeated three times. After 7 days, the students counted the seeds that had germinated and measured the mean shoot length of the germinated seedlings. The table shows the means for each treatment.

Salt concentration (g/L) | Temperature (°C) | Mean germination (%) | Mean shoot length (mm)
0 | 15 | 92 | 38
2 | 15 | 84 | 33
4 | 15 | 70 | 24
8 | 15 | 41 | 11
0 | 25 | 95 | 45
2 | 25 | 88 | 40
4 | 25 | 76 | 31
8 | 25 | 52 | 18
questions.q: At 25°C, the mean shoot length at 4 g/L was how many millimeters less than the mean shoot length at 0 g/L?
options: 14 mm
13 mm
7 mm
17 mm
questions.explanation: At 25°C, the mean shoot length was 45 mm at 0 g/L and 31 mm at 4 g/L, so the difference is 45 − 31 = 14 mm. The value 13 mm comes from comparing 4 g/L and 8 g/L at 25°C, not 0 g/L and 4 g/L.

questions.topic: Data representation: reading tables and graphs
questions.passage:
Two scientists studied algal blooms in four coves of Clearwater Lake. Dr. Vela proposed that blooms are mainly controlled by phosphorus entering the lake in runoff. Dr. Nwosu proposed that blooms are mainly controlled by water temperature. During one summer, a research team measured total phosphorus, mean water temperature, and chlorophyll a in each cove. Chlorophyll a is used as a measure of algae abundance. The coves had similar depth and light exposure, and none received direct sewage discharge. The team sampled each cove three times in July and averaged the measurements. The table shows the results.

Cove | Total phosphorus (µg/L) | Mean water temperature (°C) | Chlorophyll a (µg/L)
North | 18 | 21 | 8
East | 45 | 20 | 25
South | 20 | 27 | 19
West | 50 | 28 | 38
questions.q: According to the table, which cove had the greatest chlorophyll a concentration?
options: East
West
North
South
questions.explanation: The chlorophyll a values are 8 µg/L in North, 25 µg/L in East, 19 µg/L in South, and 38 µg/L in West. The greatest value is 38 µg/L, which occurred in West.

questions.q: To test directly whether phosphorus causes increased algae, which experimental design would be best?
options: Add phosphorus to an entire cove and compare it with the other coves.
Use tanks at different temperatures and add different amounts of phosphorus to each.
Measure phosphorus and chlorophyll a in the same four coves each week for another summer.
Fill identical tanks with lake water, keep them at the same temperature, add different amounts of phosphorus to some tanks and none to others, and measure chlorophyll a.
questions.explanation: A direct test requires manipulating phosphorus while holding other factors, especially temperature, constant. Identical tanks at the same temperature with some receiving no added phosphorus provide a control and reduce confounding. The cove observations and whole-cove addition would not separate phosphorus effects from other variables, and tanks at different temperatures would confound temperature with phosphorus.

For each trial, they mixed 2.0 mL of amylase solution with 10.0 mL of 1.0% starch solution in a buffer at 25°C. Each pH was tested twice and the times were averaged. Maya predicted that the amylase would be most active near pH 6.0, close to the pH of barley cytoplasm. Luis predicted that it would be most active near pH 4.0, like the acidic conditions in germinating seeds. Table 1 shows the average times.
pH | Average time (s)
